Capstone — Integrated Financial Analysis System

Role and two-part committee decision

You are the lead analyst. Present (1) the system's current investment/finance action and conditions and (2) whether the committee should approve, revise, defer, or reject the system for decision use. A polished dashboard alone is not an integrated system.

Points and the enforced due date appear in the Brightspace assignment header. The separate Capstone — Edition A Checkpoint (AI Closed) page publishes the synthesis-baseline window; do not use the final-assignment page as the Edition A submission location.

Planning estimate: 12–16 out-of-class hours distributed across Weeks 14–16, including interface mapping, the AI component and its validation, end-to-end tests, cold run, evidence reconciliation, writing (including the launch-post draft), recording, transcript correction, and access checks. Reused validated components reduce duplication but not integration testing.

Role and two-part committee decision
Student-work phase Target Planned effort
Nov. 19–24 Edition A receipt and component/interface choice; Project 2 remains first priority through Nov. 22 20 minutes for Edition A
Nov. 29–Dec. 1 assemble reused components into an integration skeleton; wire and guard the AI component (GenAI Studio route or documented fallback); locate current output, README, memo/deck, and validation evidence; predict one interface failure 3–4 hours
Dec. 1–3 produce the first end-to-end runnable package for a README-only cold run; draft Edition B, memo/validation updates, the launch-post draft, and three distinct video outlines 3–4 hours
Dec. 3–10 repair and retest, reconcile all surfaces, freeze output, record/correct three videos, run access checks, and submit 5–7 hours

The relevant Week 14–15 class studios supply additional guided time. The 12–16-hour estimate assumes reuse of Project 1/2 components and forbids building a new third system from scratch; if reuse is not possible, reduce scope through the published support route rather than silently exceeding the estimate. The plan assumes no required course work during Thanksgiving Break, Nov. 25–28. Students may start later phases early, but no deadline or required interaction falls in the break.

Problem statement, then — the Edition A boundary

The merged-shell window opens Thu Nov. 19 at 6:00 p.m. ET after the later section ends and closes Tue Nov. 24 at 1:30 p.m. ET at the earlier section opening. Budget 20 minutes; this is separate from the selected-track prework. Submit the separate ungraded Capstone Edition A checkpoint within that window before requesting new capstone-specific generative-AI assistance. You may draft or submit it before Project 2 closes; use the evidence available at that moment and do not delay Project 2 completion. Edition A states the committee decision, intended user, two components, material interface, initial action, known evidence, unknowns, and validation plan. Prior projects may contain disclosed AI-assisted work; identify that inherited provenance rather than making a false “no AI ever” claim. The attestation covers only the new capstone synthesis since the checkpoint window opened. Its first successful Brightspace receipt is the immutable baseline of record.

A missing or unreceipted on-time Edition A cannot be recreated or backdated. Under PROJECT-SUBMISSION-ARCHITECTURE.md and the shared analytic rubric, the missing A-to-B evidence is scored once under Problem Definition and Decision Usefulness; do not add an integrity assumption or second automatic deduction. Approved accommodations, Special Access, and late-add cases receive a documented individual window before that student's capstone-specific AI work.

Required integration

Choose one coherent public-security/issuer/portfolio decision that links:

  • at least one issuer/corporate component (valuation, operating drivers, credit/downside, or security cash-flow analysis); and
  • at least one investment component (mandate, portfolio/allocation, market/signal evidence, scenario risk, or monitoring/rebalance logic).

The selected components must exchange at least one material input or decision state. Create the Week 15 evidence graph from committee claim through source, as-of date, convention, calculation, test, action, and reversal trigger. Audit entity, date, currency, units, frequency, price basis, scenario, weight, and version at every interface. Agreement among components that share one stale input is not independent confirmation.

Fixed-income techniques may be used only if the released course track makes them available to the entire class; they are never required to earn full credit. The evidence architecture, rubric, and required integration are identical for every student.

Scope and validation

  • Reuse and improve validated work when appropriate, but disclose provenance and do not submit unchanged prior work as new integration.
  • You may repair any reused Project 1 or Project 2 component for the capstone regardless of its earlier score. Preserve the prior artifact/commit, identify the repair and evidence, and retest it. The earlier project is not reopened or regraded. A repair earns no separate points; it is evidence only for the existing Capstone criterion or criteria that the repaired component materially improves.
  • State one committee decision and a finite top-three failure budget.
  • Run at least one end-to-end changed-input test with expected direction written first.
  • Preserve that test as the Locked Changed-Input Record with a human-authored, AI-off prediction before the run, precommit timestamp/commit, old/new input and units, expected/actual output direction, decision effect, and failure diagnosis or no-change reason.
  • Test one cross-component contradiction or common-dependency failure.
  • Complete a cold run from the README and preserve visible executed output.
  • Reconcile current Edition A/B, including supported “no material change.”
  • State what the system cannot establish and the monitoring/kill/escalation process.

Required intelligence — the AI component

The system must contain at least one load-bearing generative-AI component: an LLM call inside your pipeline that does judgment-shaped work the deterministic code cannot — for example, extracting risk language from a filing, drafting the analyst commentary from your computed results, or screening candidates with stated reasoning. One call doing real work is enough; an agent platform is not required. Integration is evaluated by decision coherence and tested interfaces — never by the number of tools, APIs, pages, or agents.

The component must appear in your validation evidence like any other model: where it sits in the pipeline, what guards its output, and at least one documented case where you challenged or corrected it. "The model said so" is not evidence anywhere in this course, including here.

Access route. The primary route is Purdue GenAI Studio, which provides free OpenAI-compatible API access to Purdue students (endpoint, key setup, and worked example: RCAC GenAI Studio API guide). GenAI Studio access, keys, and API behavior are supported by RCAC, not the teaching team; the teaching team supports your finance and design decisions. If API access fails, the documented manual protocol is admissible: the exact structured prompt, the pasted model output, and your validation applied to it demonstrate the same design. The access route never changes the scoring standard.

Submission bundle

One Brightspace assignment, one manifest, six items. The shared architecture in PROJECT-SUBMISSION-ARCHITECTURE.md governs formats, filenames, transcripts, and the frozen-record rules; the capstone additions and durations below override where they differ.

Submission bundle
# Item Capstone form
1 Repository Working code, README, reproducible visible output — and the AI component identified by file/function in the manifest
2 Problem statement, then and now Edition A (the raw, timestamped checkpoint) unchanged, plus the polished Edition B — the A-to-B delta is the evidence
3 AI-aided build-process video Video 1, max 6:00 — the journey: one real failure and its diagnosis, one accept/modify/reject decision with reasoning, what AI did versus what you decided
4 Tech overview video Video 2, max 10:00 — the product: architecture, data flow, financial logic, where the AI component sits and what guards it, reproduction of the output, highest-risk validation
5 Product presentation video Video 3, max 8:00 — the committee pitch: decision first, range, evidence, risks, triggers, clear ask. No build war stories, no code tour
6 Launch-post draft ~800-word written product story, Substack-ready markdown, submitted in the bundle. Publishing it is optional, encouraged, and never graded; the draft is required

All three videos are on YouTube, Unlisted or Public — your choice, never Private — with your face on camera (the standing webcam rule and its accommodation equivalents apply), YouTube transcripts/captions enabled, and links viewable by the instructional team through the grade-appeal window. Corrected plain-text transcripts are submitted as usual. The decision memo/deck and the shared validation, manifest, and attestation templates remain required as part of the standing architecture.

Consultation studios and holistic evaluation

There is no live board and no scheduled defense. The Week 15–16 class meetings are consultation studios: formative working sessions where the teaching team pressure-tests your evidence, videos, and submission mechanics before the deadline. Studios create no points and no penalties; the final submitted bundle is the only graded object.

The capstone is evaluated holistically under the shared six-criterion analytic rubric in MAJOR-PROJECT-ANALYTIC-RUBRIC.md — there is no per-item point mapping across the six bundle items. A complete bundle earns evaluation, not points; the points come from the quality of the judgment the bundle makes visible. An incomplete bundle (missing item, private video, absent transcript, inaccessible repository) is missing evidence under the criterion it starves.
